Tremble
TREM-bul
v.
From Old French trembler, from Latin tremulus (shaking), from tremere (to shake). Renders the Hebrew rā‘ad, “to tremble, quake,” chārēd, “to tremble with awe,” and the Greek tremō, “to tremble.”

📖 Biblical Definition

To tremble in Scripture is the bodily expression of reverent fear before God—not the cringing terror of the slave before the tyrant, but the awed shaking of the creature standing in the presence of the holy Creator, the sinner standing before the throne of judgment, or the saint hearing the Word of his God with the weight that Word deserves. The pattern is set early: Israel at Sinai trembles before the voice of the LORD and the smoking mountain; Daniel in the presence of the heavenly messenger is left trembling and without strength; Isaiah in the throne-room cries woe is me, for I am undone; Habakkuk says when I heard, my belly trembled; my lips quivered at the voice; the disciples at the transfiguration were sore afraid. The LORD Himself names trembling as a mark of those He looks upon: to this man will I look, even to him that is poor and of a contrite spirit, and trembleth at my word. The New Testament continues the theme: the apostles charge the believer to work out your own salvation with fear and trembling, not because salvation is precarious but because it is awesome; James warns that even the devils believe and tremble—a fearful word against the doctrinaire who knows much and is unmoved. Trembling is no fashion of natural temperament; it is a Spirit-wrought response of the spiritually living soul to the holy God and His weighty Word. Its loss in any age is a sign that the doctrine of God has shrunk, that the holiness of God has been domesticated, and that the soul has lost the proper sense of His presence. Recover the doctrine of God in His holiness, and trembling returns of itself—the right and reverent shaking of the creature before the Creator and the sinner before the Savior in whose hand are the issues of life and death.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines TREMBLE as to shake involuntarily, as with fear, cold, or weakness; to quake; to shudder; to quiver; in scripture, to fear; to be affected with fear.

expand to see more

TREMBLE, v.i. — 1. To shake involuntarily, as with fear, cold, or weakness; to quake; to shudder; to quiver. 2. To shake; to quiver, as the earth or the heavens. 3. In scripture, to fear; to be affected with fear; as, to tremble at the word of the LORD (Isa 66:2).

TREMBLING, n. — The act of shaking involuntarily; quaking; the state of being affected with fear or reverence.

📖 Key Scripture

Philippians 2:12 — "Wherefore, my beloved, as ye have always obeyed... work out your own salvation with fear and trembling."

Isaiah 66:2 — "...but to this man will I look, even to him that is poor and of a contrite spirit, and trembleth at my word."

James 2:19 — "Thou believest that there is one God; thou doest well: the devils also believe, and tremble."

Acts 16:29 — "Then he called for a light, and sprang in, and came trembling, and fell down before Paul and Silas..."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

Trembling is corrupted by the domesticated god of the present age—reduced to a friendly companion who issues no summons that shakes the soul—and by the casual register of worship and Scripture-reading that meets the holy God with no awe and no quaking at all.

expand to see more

The shrinking of the doctrine of God in the contemporary church has produced a generation that does not tremble. Where the saint of every preceding age met the holy God in the Word and at the Lord’s table with a reverence that shook the soul, the modern worshipper meets a domesticated god who issues no summons that quakes him: a god who is endlessly affirming, endlessly understanding, endlessly tolerant of whatever the worshipper brings; a god whose voice is the gentle whisper only and never the voice that shook Sinai. The result is worship without trembling, Scripture-reading without trembling, prayer without trembling, the Lord’s table approached without trembling—and a Christianity stripped of one of the marks Scripture itself names as the credential of the regenerate soul: him that trembleth at my word.

James’ rebuke is severe and quotable: thou believest that there is one God; thou doest well: the devils also believe, and tremble. The man who knows true doctrine and is unmoved by it is in worse case than the demon who at least trembles at what he knows. Recover the holiness of God, the weight of His Word, the reality of His presence, the seriousness of His judgments—and trembling returns of itself. The recovery is not artificial: the saint cannot be talked into trembling; he can only be set, by the Spirit, in the presence of the God who summons it. But the right setting—a high doctrine of God preached and sung, a Bible read as the actual voice of God, a Lord’s table approached as a meeting with the crucified and risen Christ—will produce the trembling that the contemporary register has so notably lost.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew rā‘ad (to tremble, quake), chārēd (to tremble with awe—Isa 66:2), and rāgaz (to be agitated, tremble); Greek tremō (to tremble)—the bodily expression of reverent fear before the holy God.

expand to see more

Hebrew rā‘ad (H7460) — to tremble, quake.

Hebrew chārēd (H2729) — to tremble with awe; cognate of the noun in Isa 66:2.

Hebrew rāgaz (H7264) — to be agitated, tremble, quake.

Greek tremō (G5141) — to tremble; used of the woman with the issue of blood, of the Philippian jailer, and of the demons (James 2:19).

Usage

"The devils also believe, and tremble—the doctrinaire who knows and is unmoved is in worse case than the demon who at least trembles at what he knows."
